As You Can See Everything proves to be their Halloween-timed hit, A24 has set Jeremy Saulnier’s Halloween-themed mystery-thriller Slayground (formerly titled October ) for January, but we are at least getting the first substantial look at the film this month.

With a cast including Cory Michael Smith, Chase Sui Wonders, Sophie Wilde, James Badge Dale, Stanley Simons, Stephen Root, Chris Sullivan, Young Mazino, Imogen Poots, Matty Matheson, and Macon Blair, the first official trailer has now arrived ahead of a January 29 release.

Here’s the synopsis: “Scare-actor “Metal Mike” Graves wakes up in a haunted attraction surrounded by the dead bodies of his co-workers with no memory of how they got there. As a state-wide manhunt closes in, he races to uncover the truth – even if the trail leads straight back to him.”

See the trailer below for the film, which features a score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Beverly Hills-based film finance specialist Launch Financing is poised to scale up its short-term gap loan services for indie productions in the U.S., Canada and the UK having secured its first ever institutional $15M senior credit facility.

The film-lending arm of producer-financier Chris K. Daniels’ The Launch Company , has previously funded more than 60 media loans against tax credits, pre-sales and other committed production receivables.

Past recipient productions include thriller The Dutchman , black comedy Thumb and coming-of-age comedy The Marshmallow Experiment as well as Kristallnacht and Night Comes .

Related Stories

Eric McCormack Set For Nimisha Mukerji's Psychological Thriller 'You're Safe Now'

'Dancing With The Stars' Val Chmerkovskiy Suspended For TikTok Referencing Will Smith Oscar Moment; Dancer Responds, "Instinct Was To Defend My Wife"

The new $15 million senior credit facility has been provided by specialty lender Pier Asset Management and is Launch Financing’s first institutional warehouse facility.

Watch on Deadline

The line, extendable to $25 million over time, will enable Launch Financing to scale its short-term production lending to independent films in the U.S., Canada and the UK.

“A production’s money always comes slower than the production wants it to. Tax credits, bank closings, equity cashflow and distributor payments arrive on their own schedule, and the schedule is not the shoot’s,” said Daniels.

“We built a standardized loan structure that clears diligence in two to five business days and wires within forty-eight hours of signing, because that is the only thing a producer in prep actually needs from a lender. This facility allows us to expand beyond our current pipeline and work more closely with high-quality producers, production companies, agencies and studios, improving the process one film at a time.”

Launch Financing advances senior secured capital against money a production is set to receive and is repaid when that money arrives. Loans run eight to twenty-six weeks and are secured in first position against government production incentives, distributor minimum guarantees, pre-sales, committed equity, institutional capital and library-backed corporate guarantees.

The money typically covers production cashflow while a bank or institutional lender closes, as well as cast escrow and union deposits, production payroll and finishing funds.

Launch Financing sits inside The Launch Company alongside Launch Development, which develops and packages film projects; Cinelaunch, the company’s business-affairs and back-office platform; and Launch North, its physical production operation in Toronto.

The lending team has sat on both sides of the table, as producers who have borrowed against tax credits and pre-sales and as the institutional capital that structures those loans.

Daniels, who is also a strategic partner at Esme Grace, the boutique firm behind Michael Mann’s Ferrari , serves as chief executive officer of The Launch Company and its lending arm. Wyatt Cavalier is Launch Financing JV’s chief investment officer , and Jess Mastro is head of development for The Launch Company.

title_original: Why Georgia Oakley Didn’t Want to Modernize Jane Austen for Her New Film of ‘Sense and Sensibility’
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "English director Georgia Oakley showcased a distinctive, naturalistic style — and her ability to translate a personal story into an original script — with her freshman feature, “ Blue Jean .” The atmospheric drama followed a closeted physical ed teacher in Newcastle, navigating the introduction of Margaret Thatcher’s Section 28 anti-gay law. So a Regency period piece with an adapted screenplay already attached wasn’t the most expected choice for her second film . Yet the director delivers a fresh take on the Jane Austen classic “ Sense and Sensibility ” that fits seamlessly into her burgeoning oeuvre.", "links": [{"text": "Georgia Oakley", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/georgia-oakley/"}, {"text": "Blue Jean", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/blue-jean-review-lesbian-drama-1234872768/"}, {"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}, {"text": "Sense and Sensibility", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/sense-and-sensibility-2026-movie-review-1235221438/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I think it’s probably something to do with the fact that I love stories about outsiders,” Oakley told IndieWire, comparing Austen’s dispossessed Dashwoods to the protagonist of “Blue Jean,” whose fear about being outed and punished under the new law sends her into a self-alienating spiral. “I’m interested in characters that are living just on the edges of whatever is deemed to be the status quo of the time.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/everest_the_other_side.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "'Everest: The Other Side'", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screen-Shot-2026-09-07-at-5.18.25-PM.png?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "'Musk'", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Oakley also gravitates to stories that use a strong narrative framework to explore social issues and subvert expectations. “The framework for this story is, obviously, the romance. But at the same time, she [Jane Austen] has smuggled in all of these subversive messages about the limitations of life as a woman. And I think I’m always drawn to stories where you’re taken on a journey, but at the same time, unpacking quite loaded and resonant themes.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the central Dashwoods, sisters Elinor and Marianne, Oakley’s “ Sense and Sensibility ” is more stripped-down than its best-known predecessors, including Ang Lee’s beloved 1995 version with co-writer Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet. Though the new film, a collaboration between Working Title and Focus Features, is as faithful to the source text as any Austen lover could ask for — even those who might take issue with a softened Willoughby (“Urchin” star Frank Dillane) or a particularly self-serving Lucy Steele (Ceara Covene).", "links": [{"text": "Esmé Creed-Miles", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/sense-and-sensibility-movie-star-esme-creed-miles-interview-1235221468/"}, {"text": "Sense and Sensibility", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/sense-and-sensibility/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MCDSEAN_UC017.jpg?w=650", "alt": "SENSE AND SENSIBILITY, from left: Esme Creed-Miles, Daisy Edgar-Jones, 2026. © Focus Features / Courtesy Everett Collection", "caption": "‘Sense and Sensibility’ ©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Oakley, who studied English literature at Newcastle University, has long been a fan of Austen’s first novel for its focus on the evolving relationship between the eldest sisters and, she said, for the “wildness to it.” Like screenwriter Diana Reid, Oakley wanted to foreground the “love story between the sisters,” rather than their respective romances. Unlike some recent adaptations of classic literature, though, she didn’t feel Austen’s narrative needed updating or packaging in a contemporary way to feel relevant."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I really feel that Austen was writing about things that were so inherently contemporary that it didn’t need modernizing,” Oakley said, adding that while she wouldn’t generally classify herself as a “purist” when it comes to adaptations, she certainly leaned that way when it came to bringing “Sense and Sensibility” to the screen. “I don’t know if ‘purist’ is the right word, but there’s definitely something there in terms of not fixing what ain’t broke.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Diana wrote a screenplay where she retained, as much as possible, Austen’s actual language. She hasn’t tried to say, ‘We can only identify with these people if we bring them into the present.’ She’s said that the whole point is that we should be able to allow this story to wash over us, and to feel the connection with these characters in spite of our differences, rather than attempting to kind of close that gap. And I very much stand by that, as well,” she said. “Thematically, it [‘Sense and Sensibility’] speaks so much to what it means to be a young woman in today’s world without actually changing anything at all.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Despite foregoing a contemporary lens, Oakley, like most filmmakers given a chance to make a big studio adaptation, didn’t shy away from casting actors well known to today’s moviegoing crowd. To round out the central cast, Oakley tapped the iconic Fiona Shaw as neighborly Mrs. Jennings, “Outlander” star Caitríona Balfe as Mrs. Dashwood, “Hamnet” breakout Bodhi Rae Breathnach as the youngest Dashwood sister, and English charmer George MacKay as Elinor’s gentle-souled love interest, Edward. And even without Edgar-Jones, who is quickly becoming one of Hollywood’s most bookable young female leads, that would have been plenty of star power to contend with."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Unlike what we’ve seen more often in recent adaptations, though, the heavy-hitting co-stars mostly disappear into their characters rather than make a spectacle of them, as the director intended. “I want the audience to kind of come at these characters with as little baggage as possible,” Oakley said, explaining that she was excited by the challenge of showcasing the film’s stars — and especially Edgar-Jones, who hasn’t done a British role in years — in a way that felt novel rather than distracting. “I want the audience to get to know the characters without just thinking, ‘This is that person.’”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MCDSEAN_UC002.jpg?w=650", "alt": "SENSE AND SENSIBILITY, from left: Esme Creed-Miles, Daisy Edgar-Jones, transforming her stars into believable Georgian protagonists wasn’t the only casting-related challenge that Oakley had to overcome to realize her version of “Sense and Sensibility.” Finding the perfect candidates for the period piece’s two major locations — Norland Park, the stately home the family must vacate after Mr. Dashwood dies, and Barton Cottage, the humble abode they relocate to in remote Devon — was just as essential. “The casting of those two locations felt as weighty and as important as the casting of the two sisters,” said Oakley, who was scouting properties along the rugged coastline of Cornwall, Dorset, and Devon even before a production designer was attached to the film."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Oakley’s focus on finding the perfect settings for her comedy of manners isn’t surprising, given what she achieved production-wise with “Blue Jean,” set in a small town in the North of England in 1988. English director Georgia Oakley showcased a distinctive, naturalistic style — and her ability to translate a personal story into an original script — with her freshman feature, “ Blue Jean .” The atmospheric drama followed a closeted physical ed teacher in Newcastle, navigating the introduction of Margaret Thatcher’s Section 28 anti-gay law. So a Regency period piece with an adapted screenplay already attached wasn’t the most expected choice for her second film . Yet the director delivers a fresh take on the Jane Austen classic “ Sense and Sensibility ” that fits seamlessly into her burgeoning oeuvre.

“I think it’s probably something to do with the fact that I love stories about outsiders,” Oakley told IndieWire, comparing Austen’s dispossessed Dashwoods to the protagonist of “Blue Jean,” whose fear about being outed and punished under the new law sends her into a self-alienating spiral. “I’m interested in characters that are living just on the edges of whatever is deemed to be the status quo of the time.”

Oakley also gravitates to stories that use a strong narrative framework to explore social issues and subvert expectations. “The framework for this story is, obviously, the romance. But at the same time, she [Jane Austen] has smuggled in all of these subversive messages about the limitations of life as a woman. And I think I’m always drawn to stories where you’re taken on a journey, but at the same time, unpacking quite loaded and resonant themes.”

Starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the central Dashwoods, sisters Elinor and Marianne, Oakley’s “ Sense and Sensibility ” is more stripped-down than its best-known predecessors, including Ang Lee’s beloved 1995 version with co-writer Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet. Though the new film, a collaboration between Working Title and Focus Features, is as faithful to the source text as any Austen lover could ask for — even those who might take issue with a softened Willoughby (“Urchin” star Frank Dillane) or a particularly self-serving Lucy Steele (Ceara Covene).

Oakley, who studied English literature at Newcastle University, has long been a fan of Austen’s first novel for its focus on the evolving relationship between the eldest sisters and, she said, for the “wildness to it.” Like screenwriter Diana Reid, Oakley wanted to foreground the “love story between the sisters,” rather than their respective romances. Unlike some recent adaptations of classic literature, though, she didn’t feel Austen’s narrative needed updating or packaging in a contemporary way to feel relevant.

“I really feel that Austen was writing about things that were so inherently contemporary that it didn’t need modernizing,” Oakley said, adding that while she wouldn’t generally classify herself as a “purist” when it comes to adaptations, she certainly leaned that way when it came to bringing “Sense and Sensibility” to the screen. “I don’t know if ‘purist’ is the right word, but there’s definitely something there in terms of not fixing what ain’t broke.”

“Diana wrote a screenplay where she retained, as much as possible, Austen’s actual language. She hasn’t tried to say, ‘We can only identify with these people if we bring them into the present.’ She’s said that the whole point is that we should be able to allow this story to wash over us, and to feel the connection with these characters in spite of our differences, rather than attempting to kind of close that gap. And I very much stand by that, as well,” she said. “Thematically, it [‘Sense and Sensibility’] speaks so much to what it means to be a young woman in today’s world without actually changing anything at all.”

Despite foregoing a contemporary lens, Oakley, like most filmmakers given a chance to make a big studio adaptation, didn’t shy away from casting actors well known to today’s moviegoing crowd. To round out the central cast, Oakley tapped the iconic Fiona Shaw as neighborly Mrs. Jennings, “Outlander” star Caitríona Balfe as Mrs. Dashwood, “Hamnet” breakout Bodhi Rae Breathnach as the youngest Dashwood sister, and English charmer George MacKay as Elinor’s gentle-souled love interest, Edward. And even without Edgar-Jones, who is quickly becoming one of Hollywood’s most bookable young female leads, that would have been plenty of star power to contend with.

Unlike what we’ve seen more often in recent adaptations, though, the heavy-hitting co-stars mostly disappear into their characters rather than make a spectacle of them, as the director intended. “I want the audience to kind of come at these characters with as little baggage as possible,” Oakley said, explaining that she was excited by the challenge of showcasing the film’s stars — and especially Edgar-Jones, who hasn’t done a British role in years — in a way that felt novel rather than distracting. “I want the audience to get to know the characters without just thinking, ‘This is that person.’”

But transforming her stars into believable Georgian protagonists wasn’t the only casting-related challenge that Oakley had to overcome to realize her version of “Sense and Sensibility.” Finding the perfect candidates for the period piece’s two major locations — Norland Park, the stately home the family must vacate after Mr. Dashwood dies, and Barton Cottage, the humble abode they relocate to in remote Devon — was just as essential. “The casting of those two locations felt as weighty and as important as the casting of the two sisters,” said Oakley, who was scouting properties along the rugged coastline of Cornwall, Dorset, and Devon even before a production designer was attached to the film.

Oakley’s focus on finding the perfect settings for her comedy of manners isn’t surprising, given what she achieved production-wise with “Blue Jean,” set in a small town in the North of England in 1988. The director — who took inspiration from a slew of paintings, as well as Stanley Kubrick’s “Barry Lyndon” and Jane Campion’s “Bright Star” — is methodical in her approach to using design elements to lend authenticity and shape her films’ aesthetics.

When the group came across the West Dorset estate that would serve as the Dashwood sisters’ childhood home, for example, Oakley was drawn to how the property inherently communicated a kind of history she wanted to echo in her portrayal of Norland Park. “It was kind of grand and impressive in the way that I wanted it to be, but it also had this kind of crumbling [look]. Like, even the pattern on the front of the stone was just kind of lived-in. And so it spoke to this naturalistic feeling that I was reaching for,” the director said.

“And there was actually a young family living in the house who had inherited it, so there was some overlap, in that they weren’t really sure what to do with it or how to look after it. They’d only been there a short time, and the wallpaper was peeling, and the carpets were fraying, and it felt loved as a house, but not particularly preserved. And that was exactly what I was looking for to tap into this feeling of everything being a little bit more intimate and relatable and human,” she added.

The stand-in for Barton Cottage, a single-room house in southern Devon more suited to livestock than people, didn’t come quite so ready-made — or with a roof. After production designer Francesca Di Mottola and her team finished transforming it, and the crew brought in a small herd of animals to dot the rounds, it had the quaint atmosphere of a place that, with enough love, could become a home. But unlike the many cottages along the coast that Oakley had scouted, it still felt isolated, befitting the story and essential to her portrayal of the Dashwoods in the latter part of the film.

As the story progresses, Oakley’s adaptation, which was shot in 35mm by cinematographer Arnaud Potier (“Dead Man’s Wire”), increasingly shows the maturing Dashwood daughters reading in the fields, performing outside work, and bringing elements from the natural world indoors as they turn the small cottage into a home. And that’s not just because the sisters’ outdoor scenes lend a dreamy quality to the film, with a palette you might use to paint a pastoral landscape. Oakley, who also cited Terrence Malick’s “Days of Heaven” as a reference, felt the best way to tap into the inner lives of Austen’s young heroines was to place them in the elements.

“I did feel that it spoke to my memory of reading the book the first time. But also, I was really interested in the relationship between those young women and time and their own agency,” Oakley said, explaining that she spoke a lot with her collaborators about “what it feels like to sit in fields and wait for letters to arrive,” never knowing when or if they would.

“It’s unthinkable, almost, in today’s world — where we are bombarded with emails and updates and whatnot every five seconds — what it feels like to have time stretching out in front of you. And then, when you couple that with grief, and a family who just experienced such an enormous loss…,” she said, referring to how, while contending with the ups and downs of new romance, Elinor and Marianne are still mourning the death of their father. “I felt that nature was just going to say so much. It was going to kind of fill the spaces in terms of understanding the emotional landscape of the characters as things evolve, as the story evolves, as they move from place to place, as the seasons change.”

“Sense and Sensibility” opens in U.S. theaters from Focus Features on October 16.

article_text:
Book Review

John Berger in His Own Bruised Time

The late novelist and art critic asked Tom Overton to wait to write his biography until after his death. The result is deeply informative, deferential, and perceptive, sometimes lyrically so.

These days, we tend to take his ideas for granted: that art — making it or contemplating it — creates knowledge. That by foregrounding the processes by which we see, we can discover the mechanisms and deceptions through which we make meaning. And, of course, that it’s important to know who is footing the bill. John Berger, who died in 2017 , was famous not for challenging the Western canon but for making its revelations feel so evidently connected to everything else about life. His essays often read like personal letters, offering to us the gift of our own passions and imaginations.

Berger was an electric presence in the 1972 BBC series Ways of Seeing , in which he appears to be standing in a museum, a kind of anarchist-angel with his unruly curls and groovy white shirt, slicing a detail out of a Botticelli with a box-cutter. This is revealed to be an illusion: The “museum” is in fact a television studio set, and the Botticelli is a reproduction. Berger was making a point about how technology changed the way we interact with images, but the subtext is clear: that he was there to cut through exclusionary and pedantic framings that, even a half-century later, persist in giving art a cordoned-off quality.

A new biography, Tom Overton’s John Berger: From Life (2026), is less interested in applying the critic and Booker Prize-winning novelist’s ideas to our cultural moment, in which human creativity is vampirically extracted and homogenized by artificial intelligence, than it is in fixing him within his own bruised 20th century, shaped by modernization and imperialism. Overton and Berger met in 2009, when he donated his archive to the British Library; Overton edited two collections of Berger’s writing on art ( Portraits: John Berger on Artists and Landscapes: John Berger on Art ) and co-edited a collection of his essays on miners, The Underground Sea . Berger, whom Overton refers to as “John” throughout, granted the author permission to write his biography after his death.

The result is deeply informative, deferential, and perceptive, sometimes lyrically so. In laying his thematic groundwork, Overton tells two stories. One is about Berger’s father, who, in the aftermath of World War I, remained in France to supervise the identification and transfer of fallen soldiers’ remains, “trying to give order and meaning to death.” The other draws from Berger’s memories as a teenager during the Blitz. Each month, he and his girlfriend would walk through bombed-out London to the National Gallery, where a single masterpiece at a time was shown — a lesson in survival “by our wits and with the Old Masters,” as Berger put it.

article_text:
H ere is an impossibly elegant, poised historical vignette whose brevity and control can hardly contain its characters’ personal and historical pain. It is directed and co-written by the Polish film-maker Paweł Pawlikowski and shot in lustrous monochrome by Lukasz Zal; it is a film about exile and betrayal, the impossibility of going home and of reconciling an artist’s children to their secondary importance.

The setting is 1949 and the celebrated German novelist and Nobel laureate Thomas Mann – who fled the Nazis before the war for California exile and US citizenship – has returned home, first visiting Frankfurt (now in West Germany) to receive an award named after Goethe, whose birthplace this is. It is Goethe’s enlightened civilised wisdom and apolitical artistry Mann will pointedly evoke in his many elaborate speeches.

Mann, played with withdrawn politeness by Hanns Zischler, is accompanied by his long-suffering grownup daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller); he is received with rapturous acclaim and, given his importance, assigned a CIA liaison. But he disconcerts and embarrasses his hosts by expressing his intention to accept a second award in Weimar, where Goethe actually lived, but which is now in the communist East and perhaps tainted by its association with the chaotic Weimar republic that ushered in the Nazis. Mann greets the communist apparatchiks’ acclaim there with the same diplomatically opaque withdrawal.

In this way, Mann evidently aspires to float free from history – and in all probability to float free from that postwar America with which he can hardly have less in common – to straddle Europe’s west and east, to make an appearance in both victorious zones and to avoid a partisan political choice in this homecoming. But while this is happening, Erika – played with the usual bayonet of intelligence by Hüller – is an anguish. She deeply misses her adored brother Klaus (August Diehl), who is also a writer in American exile and suffering from depression and drug dependency. (The film in fact begins with a bleak, prose-poetic duet of loneliness between Erika and Klaus as they speak to each other on the phone.) Later, halfway through Thomas Mann’s visit, he and Erika receive some terrible news about Klaus – news that Thomas grimly intends to ignore and carry on with his triumphal tour.

And it is Klaus who takes centre stage unexpectedly. His novel Mephisto is about a vain actor who sells out to the Nazis – and so was arguably bolder in his real-life political engagement than Thomas ever cared to be – and was based on Erika’s ex-husband, the actor and Göring courtier Gustaf Gründgens (Joachim Meyerhoff), who brazenly shows up to the Frankfurt party to celebrate Thomas with a self-pitying tale about his brief stay in a Soviet prison. Gründgens also presumes to attempt banter with Erika, who slaps his face, just as Thomas in another part of the room is telling Wagner’s oleaginous grandchildren that he has no intention of supporting the return of the Bayreuth festival and says its theatre should be burned to the ground.

This rare flash of political temper cannot erase what is to become the growing “Mephisto crisis” in Thomas’s own life. It isn’t simply that he might now feel that he neglected Klaus, or that his own colossal prestige inevitably eroded Klaus’s own writerly self-belief; it is that Klaus’s great creation reproaches him. Able to move freely across the iron curtain, he can feel he is above any Mephisto-type sellout to the Americans or the Soviets, but then where is his commitment? To Germany , of course, but the Germany that was the root of his greatness (and that of Goethe) is gone; Germany is dead and perhaps Mann himself, with his American passport, is now a ghost.

At a Frankfurt press conference, Mann is reproached by one German correspondent for not having chosen the martyred path of “internal emigration” within Germany – ie mutely enduring the tyranny – rather than leaving the country. Mann does not reply that “internal emigration” is Germany’s convenient postwar myth, but crisply says that without leaving he would not have survived. Yet the film’s pathos, brought into a sharper focus by his son’s heartbreaking fate, is that survival itself is called in to question. Perhaps Mann senses that Germany’s national spirit has not survived – compromised by geopolitical division, partisan politics, cold war acrimony and the terrible memory of the Holocaust – and that its language and culture have been therefore contaminated, as suggested in books such as Hermann Broch’s The Death of Virgil and George Steiner’s Language and Silence.

It is the music of Bach that is to bring some measure of redemption and emotional release for both father and daughter, but Pawlikowski does not offer anything emollient or elegiac in this taut, literate picture.

article_text:
Seven years have passed since Cats , but the spectacular musical flop still makes Judi Dench cringe.

Writing in her new memoir, Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? , the Oscar-winner lamented the “waste” of “goodwill and talent” on Tom Hooper’s 2019 adaptation of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s stage show.

Dench says she has never watched the final version of Cats , in which she played Old Deuteronomy and had to wear a fur coat that she once described as like “five foxes f**cking on my back.”

”Oh God, I can’t bear it – and [Lloyd Webber] had waited so long for it to be made,” Dench wrote in her book. ”What a waste of all that goodwill and talent.”

Source: Universal

‘The Odyssey’

EXCLUSIVE: Universal brass confirmed on Friday (October 30) that Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey has overtaken Furious 7 and surpassed $1.17bn this week to become the studio’s highest-grossing international release of all time.

“Christopher Nolan occupies rarefied air as a filmmaker whose star power transcends borders,” Veronika Kwan Vandenberg, president of distribution, Universal Pictures International, told Screen . “This historic milestone speaks to the unyielding ambition of Chris and Emma [Thomas], delivering a cinematic achievement whose scale and craftsmanship breathe life into Homer’s epic poem.”

The adaptation of Homer’s 3,000-year-old epic about Odysseus’s decade-long return from the Trojan War to his wife Penelope in Ithaca has broken multiple records, among them: Nolan’s highest international opening (it debuted at number one in 77 markets) and international cumulative total. It also ranks as the UK director’s biggest film in 78 markets including UK & Ireland, France, Germany, Italy, Mexico, Brazil, Spain, Korea, Australia, and India.

The feature ranks as the eighth highest-grossing Hollywood film of all time, and Universal’s highest-grossing release in 45 markets including South Korea, France, Italy, Australia, The Netherlands, and India. In South Korea it ranks as the biggest Hollywood film of all time and the second biggest of all time in the market.

The Odyssey is the second highest-grossing film of 2026 internationally, behind only Spider-Man: Brand New Day. At time of writing the adventure epic had grossed the following in key territories: $118.5m in the UK & Ireland (£88.2m), $102.7m in South Korea (KRW 142.4m), $93.2m in France (€81.1m), $68.2m in Germany (€59.3m), $67.6m in Italy (€58.9m), $49.4m in Australia (AUD $70.2m), $45.2m in Spain (€39.3m), $38.6m in Mexico (Ps 668.6m), $25.9m in Brazil (BRL 132.5m), and $24.2m in India (INR 2.3bn). It has grossed $115m in China (approximately CNH 766m).

Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Charlize Theron, Samantha Morton, Zendaya, and Lupita Nyong’o star. Thomas and Nolan produced through their company, Syncopy, and Thomas Hayslip served as executive producer.

Universal became the first Hollywood studio to cross $3bn at the international box office this year – it currently stands at $3.37bn, ahead of the other studios – and the first to cross $5bn worldwide.

‘Wildwood’

A busy weekend of 15 new releases sees stop-motion title Wildwood set widest release records for both distributor Black Bear and US animation studio Laika.

Directed by Laika CEO Travis Knight, Wildwood opens in 655 cinemas, which is the biggest opening ever for Black Bear, and widest a Laika film has ever played in UK-Ireland.

The film, which had its world premiere at BFI London Film Festival this month, follows a young girl into the forests outside Portland on a quest to find her kidnapped brother. UK animation filmmaker Chris Butler wrote the screenplay, based on Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis’s 2011 novel. It is the first Laika film to receive a 12A certificate in the UK, with all previous films having been rated PG.

Wildwood is a sixth feature for Portland-based Laika, which began with Coraline in 2009, opening to £1.4m and closing on £8.7m. 2012’s ParaNorman scored a solid £6.4m from a £1.3m start; before 2014’s The Boxtrolls recorded a £1.3m opening and £8.9m total, a lifetime record for the studio; although a 2024 Coraline re-release took £3.6m, giving it a higher combined total.

Its subsequent titles Kubo And The Two Strings (£3.3m total) and Missing Link (£3.6m) have dropped back slightly. Wildwood is the company’s biggest production to date with a 15-year development, and is the longest stop-motion film ever at 131 minutes; Black Bear will be hoping this scale is reflected at the box office. The highest-grossing stop-motion film ever in the UK & Ireland is Aardman’s Wallace & Gromit: The Curse Of The Were-Rabbit , with £32m in 2005.

Lionsgate is launching Ghosts: The Possession Of Button House in 642 cinemas. The film is a continuation of the cult 2019-2023 TV series, following a group of ghosts from different historical periods who share a country house with its new occupants.

UK talents Charlotte Ritchie, Kiell Smith-Bynoe, Lolly Adefope, Mathew Baynton, Simon Farnaby and Martha Howe-Douglas are among those reprising their roles from the TV series; with the film produced by Alison Owen and Debra Hayward for Monumental Television, with Andy Brunskill and Alison Carpenter.

The Inbetweeners is the high mark for UK comedy TV shows spun off into film in recent decades, with the 2011 first film opening to £8.6m and ending on a huge £45m, the 2014 second following with £8.1m and £33.4m, and a third now in production for Netflix. Other highlights include Absolutely Fabulous: The Movie , which took £16.1m in 2016; and Ali G InDaHouse , which took £10.3m in 2002. A new film for Sacha Baron Cohen’s character, Ali G: Who Iz I? , is also out this weekend through Amazon MGM Studios.

Clay and Klara

Clayface , the third film in the relaunched DC Universe franchise, starts this weekend in 572 cinemas through Warner Bros. This is the first feature to centre on the DC Comics character, with James Watkins’s film depicting a rising Hollywood star who descends into revenge-fuelled madness when his body is transformed into clay.

Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie lead the cast; both were previously named Screen Stars of Tomorrow, in 2012 and 2017 respectively. Superman , directed by DC Studios co-CEO James Gunn, got the relaunched franchise off to a decent start last year with a £7m opening and £28.1m total. However, Supergirl struggled earlier this year, opening to £2.1m and closing out around £5.8m.

Source: Sony

‘Klara And The Sun’

Taika Waititi’s Klara And The Sun , an adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 sci-fi novel, starts in 370 cinemas through Sony. Jenna Ortega leads the cast as the titular android who tries to bond with the sick girl for whom she was purchased; with Amy Adams, Mia Tharia, Aran Murphy, Natasha Lyonne and Steve Buscemi alongside her.

It is a ninth directorial feature for Waititi, whose leading two titles are his Thor blockbusters, 2015’s Ragnarok (opened: £7.2m; closed £31.1m) and 2022’s Love And Thunder (£9.1m; £37.6m).

Families with young children have new animation options this weekend. Kazoo Films is starting Verena Fels’ Germany-Austria co-production Monster Mia , about a young girl who starts at a monster academy as the only human, in 353 sites; while Paramount has Enrique Gato’s Spanish production Tad And The Magic Lamp in 502 cinemas. Disney is also running its pre-school Disney Junior Cinema Club screenings in 568 sites on Saturday 24.

Mubi double

There is space for independent titles, including two from Mubi. Documentary Making Marie Antoinette , directed by the late Eleanor Coppola about her daughter Sofia’s directing of 2006’s Marie Antoinette , starts in six cinemas. It will have a staggered rollout over the coming weeks, ahead of a 20 th anniversary restoration of the original film from November 13 through Park Circus.

Mubi also has Fatherland in 85 cinemas, a widest opening so far for writer-director Pawel Pawlikowski, written with Henk Handloegten. The story of the relationship between writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika at the height of the Cold War won Pawlikowski the shared best director prize at Cannes.

The film has since enjoyed an extensive festival run including Sydney, Munich, Karlovy Vary, Sarajevo, Telluride and London, and should continue its acclaim into awards season, especially for Pawlikowski and Sandra Huller’s performance as Erika. Bafta- and Oscar-nominated Cold War is the director’s box office peak, with £1.1m in 2018.

Films not in the English language include Lee Chang-dong’s Venice Competition entry Possible Love , which is an awards contender as South Korea’s entry to the best international feature Oscar, for Netflix. Also out are Bollywood adventure Udta Teer on 78 screens through Moviegoers Entertainment; and comedy Godday Godday Chaa 2 through Zee Studios – the first film took £136,000 in 2023.

Glimmerama is opening Jeanie Finlay’s documentary All Rivers Spill Their Stories To The Sea , about a fisherman in North East England; while Park Circus is re-releasing 1996 horror Scream in 302 sites across the week, and Exposure has documentary Children Of The Wicker Man , in which Justin Hardy investigates his father Robin’s making of The Wicker Man .

Event cinema releases this weekend include Scottish Ballet reimagining of Romeo And Juliet titled These Violent Delights , which opened in 27 sites on Wednesday and plays in three sites this weekend. Trafalgar Releasing has BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ In Buenos Aires in 231 sites on Sunday; with a mini-festival of other K-pop concert films in 40 sites the day before. The distributor is also playing Noel Coward’s comedy play Fallen Angels in 355 cinemas across the weekend, having opened on Thursday.

Paramount’s Street Fighter and Universal-DreamWorks animation Forgotten Island lead the holdovers , with Amazon MGM Studios’ Colleen Hoover adaptation Verity looking to cross £10m this weekend.

article_text:
アガサ・クリスティーは「玄人はだし」の写真家だった──その素顔に迫る特別展が大英図書館で開催

『オリエント急行殺人事件』ほか、「ミステリーの女王」として数々の名作を生み出したアガサ・クリスティーの没後50周年を記念する大規模展が、今秋 ロンドン の大英図書館で開催される。展示会場では、薬学や 考古学 への関心のほか、 写真 愛好家としての知られざる素顔に触れることができる。

10月30日、 ロンドン の大英図書館で「Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery（アガサ・クリスティー：ミステリーの世界）」展が開幕する。主任キュレーターのルーシー・ローランドによると、クリスティーのキャリアや創作プロセスを幅広く紹介する同展は、「過去25年におけるイギリス最大規模」のものだという（2027年6月20日まで）。

展示品は、公私にわたる書簡やメモ、『そして誰もいなくなった』などの執筆に使われたレミントン社製タイプライターから10代の頃に執筆した初の短編小説『House of Beauty（ハウス・オブ・ビューティ）』のタイプ原稿、そして愛用していたコダックの写真機や 写真 アルバムまで100点以上にのぼる。しかも、アガサ・クリスティー・リミテッドとクリスティー・アーカイブ・トラストの協力で提供される初公開の品も多い。

これらは、没入型の演出が施された5つのセクション（イギリスの典型的なカントリーハウス、第1次世界大戦時にクリスティーが薬剤師助手として働いた調剤室、オリエント急行を模した列車、 考古学 の発掘現場、クリスティーの戯曲が上演されたウェストエンドの劇場）に展示される。そこで紐解かれるのは、エルキュール・ポアロやミス・マープルなどの個性的なキャラクターや名作ミステリー誕生の背景、そしてクリスティーの素顔や世界観だ。

このほか、著名な作家や放送関係者、熱心なファンへのインタビューを通じて、舞台や映画、テレビドラマシリーズとしても親しまれたクリスティーの作品が、ミステリー小説というジャンル全体に与えた影響が掘り下げられる。さらには、会場の随所にクリスティーのファンが謎解きを楽しめるようなヒントや、隠し要素が散りばめられているという。

今回の展覧会で特に興味深いのは、クリスティーが玄人はだしの写真愛好家だったことだ。20世紀初頭の暮らしぶりがわかる家族写真から、2人目の夫で考古学者のマックス・マローワンに同行して撮影した発掘現場の写真まで、彼女は10代の頃から70代まで長きにわたって写真を撮り続けている。ちなみに、考古学調査では発掘チームの公式フォトグラファーを務めるほどだった。

クリスティーの写真への関心を掘り起こした写真史の専門家でキュレーターのピッパ・オールドフィールド博士は、小説のプロットにおいても写真が重要な役割を果たしていると指摘する。たとえば、『茶色の服の男』（1924）のキーアイテムは謎めいた写真フィルムの容器で、ミス・マープル・シリーズの『鏡は横にひび割れて』（1962）では、ある写真が犯人の動機や正体を解き明かす手がかりであることを フィナンシャル・タイムズ紙 に語っている。

今回展示される写真は、クリスティー・アーカイブ・トラストが所蔵する資料のごく一部だが、オールドフィールド博士は日本のデザイン史家・菅靖子と共同で、クリスティーの写真に特化した展覧会の企画を進めているという。開催は来年、大英図書館のエントランスホールで行われる予定だ。

Ganadores del Ariel, Cannes y Morelia ya leen guiones de autores nuevos en Escaleta

Cine PREMIERE

La plataforma mexicana nació en octubre y en unas semanas pasó de cuatro a dieciocho lectores con nombre. Cualquier guionista puede subir su guion gratis y elegir quién se lo lee; hasta el 30 de noviembre, los primeros 50 reciben 50 dólares para su primera lectura.

Un guion casi nunca llega solo al escritorio de quien puede filmarlo. Antes alguien lo lee, lo resume y dice si vale la pena. Para un autor nuevo, sin agente ni contactos en la industria, conseguir esa primera lectura suele ser la parte más difícil del camino.

Escaleta , una plataforma mexicana lanzada en octubre de 2026, quiere que esa puerta deje de depender de a quién conoces. Quien escribe sube su guion, registrado o no, y elige a qué cineasta con trayectoria le pide una lectura por escrito. Sin convocatorias y sin esperar a que alguien conteste un correo: el precio, el plazo y la filmografía de cada lector están a la vista antes de pagar.

De cuatro a dieciocho lectores en unas semanas

La plataforma arrancó con cuatro lectores y hoy tiene dieciocho. Hay directores, guionistas y productores, muchos con más de un oficio, y una script doctor. La mayoría trabaja en México, de la Ciudad de México a Guadalajara, Monterrey, Puebla, Cuernavaca y Durango, y ya se sumaron lectores desde Santiago de Chile y Buenos Aires. Cada perfil muestra la filmografía y los premios de quien lee, tomados de IMDb.

La lista tiene peso. Salvador Aguirre ganó tres premios en Cannes en 2002 por «De Mesmer, con amor o Té para dos» y tiene un Ariel de Oro a Mejor Película por «Bajo California: el límite del tiempo». Guadalupe Ortega fue premiada en los Ariel de 1991 por «Rojo amanecer». Marcelo Tobar ganó mejor película en el Festival Internacional de Cine de Morelia 2017 con «Oso polar», y Pablo Pérez Lombardini fue premiado en Morelia en 2025 y en los Ariel de 2026 por «La reserva». El productor Yossy Zagha está detrás de «Sin señas particulares», Ariel de Oro a Mejor Película en 2021.

También leen Juan Carlos Carrasco, Ariel de Plata en 1998 por el cortometraje documental «José Barrientos»; Lucia Diaz, Premio Coral del Festival Internacional del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano de La Habana en 2015 por «Casa Blanca»; Alan Coton, Diosa de Plata especial en 2009 por «Nesio»; Luis Armando Sosa Gil, con mención especial en Morelia 2022 por «Hombres de Sal», y Miguel Valdez-López, Remi de Plata en WorldFest Houston 2020 por «El árbol».

«En unas semanas pasamos de cuatro a dieciocho lectores y siguen llegando solicitudes. Que a un guionista que empieza lo lea alguien que ganó un Ariel o un premio en Cannes le cambia la forma de reescribir», dice Herminio Ciscomani, fundador de Escaleta.

Cómo funciona una lectura

Cada lector fija su precio, desde 50 dólares (muchos rondan los 75), y su plazo de entrega, que en algunos casos es de un día. Muchos ofrecen además un modo express, que cuesta más y llega antes. El lector tiene 72 horas para aceptar el pedido; si no lo hace, el pago se devuelve completo. El dinero queda retenido hasta que el autor recibe la lectura y la acepta, y si no llega a tiempo, también se reembolsa. El lector se queda con el 80% del precio.

Lo que recibe el autor es un informe con secciones fijas: una sinopsis del guion en palabras del lector, que demuestra que lo leyó completo; fortalezas y áreas de mejora con escenas o páginas concretas; cinco áreas calificadas del 1 al 10 (premisa, estructura, personajes, diálogo, y mundo y tono); una lectura de mercado con comparables; tres cambios concretos para la siguiente versión, y un veredicto con las tres opciones que usa la industria: pasa, considerar o recomienda. Cada sección tiene una extensión mínima, el sitio no acepta entregas incompletas y la lectura la escribe el lector, sin inteligencia artificial. Después, el autor puede hacerle una pregunta por escrito.

De la nota a la segunda versión

La apuesta de Escaleta está en lo que pasa después. El autor sube la nueva versión a la misma página, con su propia etiqueta, y cada lectura indica qué versión leyó. Puede pedirle otra lectura al mismo lector o a otro, y de cada lector cuenta su calificación más reciente: la nota sigue a la reescritura. La plataforma lo recuerda con un dato en su sitio: Guillermo Arriaga reescribió «Amores perros» 36 veces.

Dos calificaciones que no se compran

Cada guion puede tener dos calificaciones, siempre separadas. La de expertos es el promedio de sus lectores con nombre; la de la comunidad, el promedio de las reseñas de otros guionistas verificados, y aparece a partir de tres reseñas. Pagar una lectura no compra la nota, y el autor no puede esconder una lectura y mostrar otra: la calificación de expertos se muestra completa o no se muestra. Los guiones que reúnen 8 o más con al menos dos lectores y 7.5 o más con al menos tres reseñas reciben el sello Certificado Escaleta.

Publicar en la comunidad es gratis: un guion aprobado queda en línea sin fecha de fin, otros guionistas pueden reseñarlo y, con tres reseñas, entra al Top de la comunidad. La página pública de cada guion muestra el título, la logline, la sinopsis y las calificaciones. El texto completo no es público: lo abren las personas que el autor contrata o invita y los usuarios verificados de la plataforma, y el autor ve en su cuenta quién lo abrió. Los datos de contacto no van en el PDF; si alguien quiere hablar con el autor, lo pide por Escaleta y el autor decide.

Crédito para la primera lectura

Hasta el 30 de noviembre de 2026, los primeros 50 escritores que confirmen su correo, suban su guion y conecten una tarjeta, sin cargo, reciben 50 dólares de crédito para su primera lectura. Si el lector cobra más, pagan la diferencia, y el crédito vence 30 días después de activarse. Cuando una lectura se completa, el guion se publica sin costo durante tres meses o más, según el precio de la lectura.

Registro, guías y plantillas

Subir un guion no requiere registro de obra. Quien ya lo tiene sube su certificado del INDAUTOR, del WGA u otro registro y, si coincide con el título y el autor, el guion lleva la etiqueta «Registro verificado»; quien no lo tiene aparece con «Registro pendiente» y puede agregarlo después. Cada guion aprobado recibe además una constancia de depósito de Escaleta.

La plataforma publica también guías gratuitas para escribir cine, del formato a la sinopsis, con plantillas descargables en Word, Excel, PDF y Fountain. Las más recientes explican cómo escribir una sinopsis, cómo usar el flashback, los tipos de conflicto y cómo construir un plot twist.

«Queríamos que alguien que escribe desde cualquier ciudad pudiera pedirle una lectura a una persona que ha hecho cine, sin depender de a quién conoce», resume Ciscomani. Para empezar basta con crear una cuenta, subir el guion en PDF y elegir lector en el directorio. Se paga en dólares con tarjeta, y el banco de cada autor hace la conversión a pesos.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Louis Partridge , the English actor best known for Enola Holmes and House of Guinness , will star in and produce the coming-of-age indie film One Last Summer .

Partridge will be joined by Mia Jenkins ( Love Me Love Me , Geek Girl ) and Jude Carmichael ( Dear England at The National Theatre), with further cast to be announced.

Written and directed by Misha Citron, whose credits include Enola Holmes, filming on One Last Summer wrapped in Tuscany, Italy. Partridge and Citron have co-founded Pipe Dream Films, which housed the One Last Summe r production.

Related Stories

Louis Partridge & Anson Boon Set For British Coming-Of-Age Film 'Andy & Orson'; MetFilm Launches Sales For TIFF Market

Mckenna Grace, Paul Walter Hauser & Louis Partridge To Star In Rom-Com 'The Official Mistress' About Final Days Of The French Monarchy - Cannes Market

Here’s the logline: “Set over a weekend in the Tuscan countryside, One Last Summer follows Milo (Partridge), who returns to the house of his late, estranged father with his best friend Zac (Carmichael).

Watch on Deadline

“Milo is convinced into a double date with two American travellers that starts strong but sharply unravels. Each character must reckon with their past selves, who they are now, and what they’re leaving behind in Italy. The film captures the intensity of brief relationships in youth.”

Jim Parks, producer of Steven Soderbergh’s The Christophers , produces alongside Maya Nurmohamed and Saskia Steinberg of Blue Lobster Productions.

Partridge said: “As an actor and a first-time producer, I loved leaning into true creative collaboration. Our aim being to make the film for ourselves, as young people to enjoy first and foremost. In doing so we hope to create something simultaneously specific and with universal scope.”

Citron added: “I wanted to create a dynamic between the ensemble that reflected the charge and intimacy of youth, feeling the sweetness of attraction that is cruelly muddied by inevitable insecurity, fear, and, often unfortunately at this age, grief.”

Partridge is repped by Independent Talent Group and WME. Jenkins is repped by Alexander Cooke at B-Side Management & Alissa Vradenburg at Untitled Entertainment. Carmichael is repped by Alexi Stylianou at 42 Management & Production.

Chris DeFaria , the former president of animation and innovative technology at Warner Bros. and producer of “ Coyote vs. Acme ,” shared his thoughts on the sudden death of Eric Bauza , the voice of many “Looney Tunes” characters.

I’m heartbroken to share that my friend and colleague Eric Bauza passed away last night. The world lost a great voice.

Eric carried the legacy of Looney Tunes with a devotion few bring to their work. He voiced Daffy Duck, Bugs Bunny, Porky Pig, Marvin the Martian, and so many more. And he never treated them as a job. To him, they were icons who deserved to be honored, protected, and kept alive for new generations. He championed these characters tirelessly in every room he walked into.

Eric never forgot whose shoulders he stood on either. He had enormous reverence for Mel Blanc, the master who gave these characters their original voices, and he used to say he was only borrowing Mel’s Cadillac, and that he promised to return the keys when he was done. That was Eric.

A man handed one of the great legacies in animation, who treated it as a trust rather than a trophy. He drove it with love and cared with a little bit of mischief, and he left it in better shape than when he found it.

After Mel’s passing in 1989, the voices he carried by himself were divided among many talented performers.

Then Eric came along.

He started by trying a few of the voices, and in what felt like no time at all, he was doing nearly all of them. It’s a feat that few, if any, had pulled off since Mel himself.

But what Eric achieved went far beyond impressions. Learning the sound of a character is hard enough. Eric did something deeper.

He learned to be them, to think like Bugs, to scheme like Daffy, to stutter and squirm like Porky. That’s why they never sounded like imitations when he performed them. They sounded alive.

What made it more remarkable was that his talent was largely his own. He was self-taught, and he built that astonishing range through curiosity, relentless practice, and a deep love of the craft. You could hear that love in every line. I was lucky enough to share time with Eric at Warner Brothers, and luckier still to have worked alongside him most recently on “Coyote vs Acme.”

Eric had a devilish wit, and was never more alive than when he stepped into those characters with a mischievous spark that made them feel new while honoring everyone who came before them.

And yes, Eric was always late. I like to think that somewhere right now, Bugs, in fact, is tapping his foot and checking his watch, and Eric is strolling in with a grin, a perfect excuse in a line so funny that all is forgiven within seconds.

He was worth the wait every single time.

Thank you, Eric, for the laughter, the artistry, the joy you gave us all. I know you promised to return Mel’s keys when you’re done. Take your time. You always did.

— As told to Jazz Tangcay

Cannes 2026 has arrived, and the Film Comment crew is on the ground, ready to cut through the noise with dispatches, interviews, Podcasts, a special Cannes Critics’ Grid, and much more. This year’s edition is packed with highly anticipated premieres from Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, Valeska Grisebach, James Gray, Paweł Pawlikowski, and many more acclaimed filmmakers.

For the second of our daily Podcasts from the Croisette, critics Katie McCabe ( Sight and Sound ) and Alison Willmore ( New York , Vulture) join FC editor Devika Girish to talk over their recent festival viewing. They begin with Pawlikowski’s highly anticipated Fatherland (3:20), before moving to Kôji Fukada’s subtle Nagi Notes (11:30), Asghar Farhadi ’s surprisingly soapy Parallel Tales (19:56), and Maxence Voiseux’s documentary Gabin (27:30) before wrapping up by revisiting Jane Schoenbrun ’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (31:52).
